trail: Fetched the raw wikitext of Wikiquote’s Mother Teresa page ↗. The line sits in the sourced 1970s section, cited to Muggeridge’s Something Beautiful for God (1971), with the citation linking to page 73 of the book.
Confirmed the book’s details against Wikipedia’s article on it ↗: a 1971 book by Malcolm Muggeridge about Mother Teresa, based on a 1969 BBC documentary of the same name.
Checked Wikiquote’s Misattributed section for Mother Teresa. It flags the “People are often unreasonable…” text as Kent M. Keith’s Paradoxical Commandments, but raises nothing against this line.

We could not read Something Beautiful for God ourselves — every copy on the Internet Archive is lending-restricted — so our citation names the book without a page, and the page-73 locator above is reported as Wikiquote’s, not as our own reading.
source.excerptNote: Mother Teresa ran a home for the dying in Calcutta and treated leprosy patients, so the comparison was not rhetorical for her — she is measuring loneliness against the two diseases she dealt with daily.

author.bio: Mother Teresa, born Anjezë Gonxhe Bojaxhiu in Skopje, founded the Missionaries of Charity in Calcutta in 1950 and spent nearly fifty years running homes for the dying, the abandoned and people with leprosy. She won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979 and was canonised in 2016. Her private letters, published in 2007, revealed decades of religious doubt that almost nobody around her had suspected.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Muggeridge went to Calcutta as a sceptic and came back a convert to her cause; his BBC film and then this book are, more than anything else, what turned a little-known nun into an international figure. The sentence is from that first introduction of her to a Western audience.

It is also a deliberate provocation aimed at that audience. Leprosy and the dying were what her order actually worked among. Telling comfortable Western readers that the worse affliction was the one they had at home — the feeling of being unwanted — was the point.
detailsBody: Muggeridge was not an uncomplicated witness. He had been the Guardian’s Moscow correspondent and one of the few Western journalists to report Stalin’s famine in Ukraine; he was also, by his own account, an agnostic when he arrived in Calcutta, and he entered the Catholic Church in 1982.

Christopher Hitchens later attacked both the book and its author at length in The Missionary Position, arguing that Muggeridge’s enthusiasm did much to build a reputation he thought unearned. That argument is about Mother Teresa’s legacy, not about whether she said this sentence — which nobody disputes.

Something Beautiful for God is a 1971 book by Malcolm Muggeridge about Mother Teresa, based on a 1969 BBC documentary of the same name.
Malcolm Muggeridge was a British journalist, formerly the Guardian’s Moscow correspondent, who entered the Catholic Church in 1982.
Mother Teresa (1910–1997) founded the Missionaries of Charity and won the 1979 Nobel Peace Prize.
The Missionaries of Charity operated homes for the dying and leprosy work in Calcutta.
